name: decorator
intent: Attach additional responsibilities to an individual object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface, so behaviour is composed per instance instead of being frozen into a subclass hierarchy.
problem: A class has to carry optional, combinable behaviour - logging, caching, retry, compression, encryption, validation - and extending it by subclassing explodes into one class per feature combination; worse, the type may be sealed, final, generated or third-party and therefore closed to modification at all, while callers need the added behaviour per instance and per configuration - decided at runtime by settings, feature toggles or call site - rather than for every object of that class.
context: Object-oriented code with a stable component interface whose behaviour must be extended orthogonally to its core responsibility: I/O and data pipelines, request and service pipelines with cross-cutting concerns, and any place where the feature set of an instance is decided at runtime (configuration, feature toggles, per-request policies) or where the same object needs different feature sets in different call sites. Works best when clients can be written against the interface and when the composition is owned by one place - a factory or composition root - rather than scattered.
benefits: Composition replaces combinatorial subclassing: N decorators cover the combinations that would need up to 2^N subclasses, and the same wrappers compose in any order.
Open/closed in practice: new behaviour is added without editing the component, which is the only route when the type is sealed, final, generated or third-party.
One responsibility per wrapper keeps classes small: the component stays free of feature flags and the cross-cutting concern lives in a named, reusable object.
Pay-as-you-go: each instance pays only for the layers it is wrapped in, and layers can be attached or omitted per instance at runtime.
Transparency: the decorator conforms to the component interface, so existing client code needs no change and decorated and undecorated objects are interchangeable.
Layers are separately testable - against a stub component or around a real one - so tests compose exactly the stack under test.
tradeoffs: A decorated object is not the wrapped object: identity comparisons, `instanceof`/casts and anything that inspects the concrete type see the outermost wrapper, so code that relies on identity or type must be rewritten or given explicit accessors.
Designs end up with many small, look-alike objects; stack traces, debugger views and log output span several layers, which makes faults harder to localise.

Forwarding is an obligation: every operation that should pass through must be implemented and kept in sync, a wide interface turns the abstract decorator into boilerplate, and a forgotten pass-through silently drops behaviour (delegation features such as Kotlin's `by` or Go embedding exist to remove this cost).
The wrapping order is semantic but implicit: a retry inside a cache behaves differently from a cache inside a retry, and nothing in the type system records or checks the intended combination.

Behaviour can only be added at the interface boundary: state or methods introduced by a decorator are unreachable through the component type without a downcast, and removing a responsibility at runtime means rebuilding the chain rather than detaching one layer.
Per-layer indirection costs a virtual/closure hop per call and, in most languages, an allocation per layer - negligible for I/O-bound work, visible on hot paths where composition could be static.

participants.responsibility: Declares the interface shared by the concrete component and every decorator; clients depend only on it, which is what makes decorated and undecorated objects interchangeable.
The object that receives the added responsibilities; implements the core behaviour and knows nothing about the decorators around it.

Abstract base that holds (or references) a Component and conforms to Component, forwarding every operation to the held instance; it exists so concrete decorators override only the operations they augment.
Adds one responsibility, running it before, after or around the forwarded call, and keeps whatever state that responsibility needs.
Builds and holds the wrapper stack, decides the composition order, and uses the composed object exclusively through the Component interface.

use_cases: I/O and data pipelines: buffering, compression, encryption, checksumming, and line-ending conversion wrapped around readers/writers (java.io FilterInputStream, Python io.TextIOWrapper/GzipFile/BufReader chains, std::streambuf filters, Node.js transform streams).

Service and repository decorators: cross-cutting behaviour — caching, retry, metrics, authorisation, validation — layered around an interface implementation at the composition root (DI-registered decorators, Go middleware, tower layers, Python decorators on Flask route handlers).

Request pipelines: authentication, rate-limiting, CORS, logging, compression, and tracing decorators wrapped around HTTP handlers (Express/Koa middleware, ASP.NET Core middleware, NestJS guards/interceptors, Spring AOP aspects).

UI and rendering: borders, scrollbars, shadows, drag-and-drop, or zoom decorators on widgets; composable visual adornments instead of a combinatorial class hierarchy (Swing/AWT, Qt event filters, React higher-order components, Angular decorators).
Evolving or sealed types: adding behaviour to final/sealed/generated/third-party classes where subclassing is impossible; toggling optional behaviour per instance for test doubles or staged rollouts.

Python function decoration: @staticmethod, @classmethod, @property, @functools.lru_cache, @functools.singledispatch, @abc.abstractmethod — language-level decorator idioms that follow the same wrapper pattern.

TypeScript/ES2022+ class decorators: meta-programming via the TC39 Stage 3 (target, context) signature to annotate or modify class elements, method descriptors, and field initialisers (Angular @Component, NestJS decorators, MobX observables).

Feature flags and runtime policies: composing behaviour variants per request or per tenant without recompiling; the same component implementation wrapped with different decorator stacks in different environments.
Legacy system bridging: wrapping a third-party or generated client with a decorator that adapts the wire format, adds retry logic, or injects authentication without modifying the generated code.

Spring Framework task execution: TaskDecorator wraps each Runnable submitted to a TaskExecutor for logging or context propagation around run(), and CompositeTaskDecorator stacks several decorators around one task (ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator since 6.1).

Django views: django.views.decorators modules (require_POST, etag, gzip_page, cache_control/never_cache) apply per-view policy decorators, and the ordered MIDDLEWARE list wraps request/response processing in an explicitly order-sensitive decorator-like chain.

Rails presentation layer (Draper): Draper::Decorator classes wrap Active Record models as view models, with delegate_all forwarding the whole model interface so views treat decorated and undecorated models interchangeably - or explicit delegate calls to narrow the exposed surface instead.
avoid_when: Only one behaviour will ever be added and it is known at design time: a subclass, a constructor parameter or a Strategy collaborator is simpler and keeps the call path direct.

The component interface is wide: forwarding boilerplate grows with it - prefer replacing the algorithm (Strategy) or use a language whose delegation support removes the forwarding (Kotlin `by`, Go embedding, Python `__getattr__`, Ruby SimpleDelegator).

Clients depend on identity or concrete type: code does `==`, `instanceof` or casts on the component, uses it as a map key, or hands out the unwrapped reference elsewhere - wrapping changes what those checks see.
The intent is a different interface (Adapter), access control or lifecycle management of the same interface (Proxy), or pure aggregation (Composite) - a decorator must preserve the contract it wraps.
Composition is fixed at compile time and performance is critical: static composition (template mixins, stackable traits, compile-time policy injection) avoids the indirection entirely.
anti_patterns: Interface-changing decorator: adding, removing, or renaming operations turns the pattern into an Adapter; substitutability breaks and clients written against the component interface can no longer use the decorated object.
Decorator-as-feature-flag: conditional behaviour still lives inside the component (if (debug) log()); nothing is composed, the component stays cluttered, and the pattern name is applied incorrectly.
Undocumented ad-hoc stacking: order-dependent decorators assembled at multiple call sites without a single place recording the intended combination; behaviour silently varies by call site.
Identity-dependent clients: code that casts to concrete type, uses the object as a map key, or serialises it will break when a decorator is inserted.
Decorator sprawl: reaching for Decorator for every variation, including cases where a constructor parameter or a Strategy swap expresses the same variation with zero extra objects and no indirection.

Decorator chains for core business logic: decorating business-rule objects with five or more layers of infrastructure concerns obscures the domain model and makes the code harder to reason about than the inheritance hierarchy it replaced.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance: behaviour is assembled from objects at runtime instead of being frozen into a class hierarchy.
Open/closed principle: the component is extended without being modified.
Single responsibility principle: each wrapper carries exactly one concern, so feature combinations do not accumulate in one class.
Liskov substitution and behavioural transparency: a decorator must remain usable - contract included, not just signatures - wherever the component is.
Interface segregation pays off twice: the narrower the component interface, the cheaper the forwarding obligation.
best_practices: Keep the component interface narrow; decoration cost (indirection + allocation per layer) grows with every forwarded operation.

Implement pass-through delegation in one base decorator class — or use language delegation (Kotlin by, Go interface embedding, Python __getattr__, Ruby SimpleDelegator) — so concrete decorators override only the operations they augment.
Document and enforce stack order in a factory or composition root; the same wrappers in different orders can produce different semantics (retry inside cache is not the same as cache inside retry).

In Python, always use functools.wraps(wrapped) on wrapper functions to preserve __name__, __doc__, __module__, __annotations__, and __qualname__; without it, introspection tools (debuggers, IDEs, inspect.signature, Sphinx) see the wrapper instead of the original.

Expose __wrapped__ (functools.update_wrapper sets it automatically) to let tools bypass the decorator for profiling, caching, or re-wrapping; boltons.funcutils.wraps or wrapt are more robust for complex signatures.
Keep decorators stateless or thread-safe: per-call state belongs to the call frame; shared counters/caches need synchronisation or per-instance storage.
Prefer explicit unwrapping accessors (getInner/into_inner) over type casting, and avoid using decorated objects as dict keys or in identity comparisons.
Test each decorator in isolation against a stub component, and test at least one composed chain for call-order correctness; layer tests catch forwarding drift, chain tests catch ordering mistakes.
In TypeScript/JavaScript, use the TC39 Stage 3 (target, context) two-argument decorator signature; avoid legacy experimentalDecorators in new code.

In NestJS and similar framework code, centralise repeated decorator compositions into factory helpers rather than scattering @UseGuards + @UseFilters + custom decorators across every controller method.

Apply security-oriented decorators (authentication, input validation, rate limiting) as the outermost layers so they execute before any privileged operation runs; logging and metrics decorators are typically innermost.

Treat decorator stacking as a finite resource: chains beyond three to five layers signal a design problem — the component interface may be too broad, the concerns may not be truly orthogonal, or a chain-of-responsibility pipeline may be more appropriate.

https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/decorator — Full pattern description with Java/C++/Python/TypeScript examples, UML diagrams, and real-world analogies.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decorator_pattern — Community-reviewed overview with applicability trade-offs and implementation notes.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html — Official Python documentation for functools.wraps and update_wrapper, the standard way to preserve introspection metadata in Python decorators.
https://hynek.me/articles/decorators/ — Please Fix Your Decorators: thorough analysis of introspection breakage in naive Python decorators and the correct functools.wraps pattern.

https://grahamdumpleton.me/posts/2014/01/how-you-implemented-your-python/ — Graham Dumpleton: common Python decorator mistakes, __wrapped__ attribute, and robust alternatives (wrapt, boltons.funcutils).
https://tc39.es/proposal-decorators/ — Official TC39 Stage 3 Decorators proposal for ECMAScript; defines the (target, context) two-argument decorator signature for JavaScript/TypeScript.

https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/main/src/lib/decorators.d.ts — TypeScript built-in decorator type definitions including ClassMethodDecoratorContext with kind, name, static, private, access, and addInitializer.
https://python-patterns.guide/gang-of-four/decorator-pattern/ — Python-specific Gang-of-Four pattern implementation guide with attention to Python idioms and pitfalls.
https://www.baeldung.com/java-structural-design-patterns — Baeldung: practical comparison of Decorator, Proxy, Adapter, and Bridge structural patterns with Java examples.
https://skillforge.aiprojects.danbla.com/topics/design-patterns-essentials — Decorator Hell discussion: deep stacking pitfalls, ordering semantics, and debugging complexity.

https://toxigon.com/mastering-the-decorator-pattern-in-c-sharp-net-8-advanced-use-cases-and-best-practices — C# .NET 8 decorator pattern: cross-cutting concerns, middleware pipelines, and decorator hell avoidance.

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/io/BufferedInputStream.html — Official Java SE documentation describing BufferedInputStream as a stream decorator (wrapper) over another InputStream with mark/reset; FilterInputStream is the abstract decorator base.

https://dev.java/learn/java-io/reading-writing/decorating/ — Official Java I/O tutorial 'Decorating I/O Streams': composing BufferedReader, GZIPInputStream and DataInputStream wrappers around readers and streams.

https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/integration/scheduling.html — Spring Framework reference: TaskDecorator wrapping submitted Runnables (logging, context propagation) and CompositeTaskDecorator chaining.
https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/decorators/ — Official Django view decorators: require_http_methods, etag, gzip_page, cache_control/never_cache applied per view.
https://github.com/drapergem/draper/blob/master/README.md — Draper README: Rails presentation decorators with delegate_all and fine-grained delegate for the wrapped model.

https://medium.com/better-programming/the-decorator-pattern-why-i-stopped-using-it-and-the-alternative-2ae447f9de08 — Critique: hidden layered behaviour makes decorators easy to overlook during refactoring; advocates embedding or injecting the logic and end-to-end testing when decorating.

https://glinteco.com/en/post/the-hidden-cost-of-python-decorators-in-production/ — Misuse analysis: chained decorators hide execution flow, roughly double call cost, and make Sentry/Datadog/OpenTelemetry report wrapper locations instead of the original function.
